Typed debounce and throttle

Debounce waits until the calls stop for wait ms. Throttle runs the function at most once per interval (this version fires on the leading edge). Because the generic is the argument tuple, the wrapped function keeps its exact parameter types.
Generic groupBy
K extends PropertyKey (string, number or symbol) lets literal key types flow through to the result. O(n).
DeepReadonly and DeepPartial utility types

These are recursive conditional and mapped types. Functions are left as they are, arrays are handled separately so they keep their element types, and primitives end the recursion. The built-in Readonly and Partial only go one level deep.
Type-safe event emitter

An event map ties each event name to its payload type, so the on and emit calls are checked at compile time. Returning an unsubscribe function helps prevent memory leaks, for example in Angular ngOnDestroy.
Discriminated-union reducer with an exhaustiveness check

The type field narrows action in each case, so action.text is only allowed under 'add'. Assigning to never makes a newly added action type fail to compile until it is handled. Every case returns a new state object and never changes the old one.
Fetch wrapper with generics and error handling

fetch doesn't reject on 4xx or 5xx responses, so check res.ok. The Result union makes the caller handle both outcomes, and AbortController adds a timeout. The as T cast is not checked at runtime, so validate the data with zod when it comes from an untrusted source.
Implement Promise.all (typed)

Store each result by its index so the output order matches the input order. Count down the ones still pending, and reject as soon as any promise rejects. A mapped type over the tuple gives each position its own awaited type.
Generic memoize

The wrapped function keeps its parameter and return types. JSON.stringify is fine as a default key for primitive arguments, but pass a custom keyFn for objects. Use a WeakMap when the key is a single object, and add an LRU limit if the cache could grow forever. If fn returns a promise, the promise itself is cached, which also removes duplicate requests that are still in flight.
User-defined type guards and assertion functions

Built-in narrowing works with typeof, instanceof, in and discriminant checks; a type predicate (p is Dog) lets you put that logic in a reusable function. An assertion function (asserts v is T) narrows by throwing instead of returning a boolean. The compiler trusts your predicate, so a wrong implementation creates a silent lie; validate external data (API responses) with a schema library such as Zod.
Implement Pick, Omit, Partial, Readonly, Record and ReturnType yourself

Three building blocks cover almost all utility types: mapped types ([K in keyof T], with ?, -? and readonly modifiers), conditional types (T extends U ? X : Y, which distribute over unions), and infer to capture a type inside a pattern. keyof any is string | number | symbol.
satisfies and as const for type-safe config objects

A type annotation widens the value to the declared type; satisfies only checks it against the type and keeps the narrower inferred type, so you get both validation and autocomplete on the real keys. as const makes literals readonly and non-widening, which is the standard way to derive a union type from a runtime array (a lightweight alternative to enum).
Branded (nominal) types: stop mixing up UserId and OrderId

TypeScript is structurally typed, so two aliases of number are interchangeable. Intersecting with a phantom __brand property makes them distinct at compile time with zero runtime cost. Combine it with a validating constructor ("parse, don't validate") so that a value of type Email is guaranteed to have been checked.
Template literal types and key remapping: generate getters and event names

Template literal types build string unions from other types (and multiply out unions). The as clause in a mapped type renames keys, and mapping a key to never removes it. Combined with infer they can parse strings at the type level, which is how routers type their path parameters.
Function overloads: different return types for different inputs

Callers see only the overload signatures, never the implementation signature, which must be compatible with all of them. Overloads are checked top to bottom, so put the most specific first. Prefer a union parameter when the return type doesn't depend on the input; use overloads (or a conditional type) when it does.
Generic LRU cache class

A JS Map iterates in insertion order, so deleting and re-inserting a key on access makes the first key the least recently used: O(1) for get and set. The generics keep keys and values type-safe at every call site. Use has rather than checking get(key) !== undefined, because undefined could be a legitimately stored value.
enum vs string-literal union vs const object

Unions are the lightest option and work with JSON from an API directly. Use the const-object pattern when you also need the values at runtime (to loop over them or build a dropdown). Enums are fine, but numeric enums have surprises (reverse mappings, loose number assignment before TS 5.0), and const enum does not work with isolated-module builds. Many style guides, and the erasableSyntaxOnly option, discourage enums for this reason.
type alias vs interface: which do you use?

| interface | type
Object shapes | Yes | Yes
Unions, tuples, primitives, mapped and conditional types | No | Yes
Declaration merging (same name twice) | Yes, merges | No, duplicate identifier error
Extending | extends, conflicts are errors | & intersection, conflicts can become never
Implemented by a class | Yes | Yes, if it is an object type
Rule of thumb: interface for object contracts (DTOs, services, public APIs that others may extend); type for unions, utility and computed types. Consistency inside a codebase matters more than the choice.
any vs unknown vs never

| any | unknown | never
What can be assigned to it | Everything | Everything | Nothing
Can be assigned to | Everything | Only unknown and any | Everything
Use it without checks | Yes, type checking is off | No, narrow first (typeof, guard) | Code is unreachable
Typical place | Migration from JS, last resort | JSON.parse results, catch (e), API input | Exhaustive switch, functions that always throw
Rule of thumb: replace any with unknown at the edges of your app and narrow once; never is the type of "this cannot happen".
Optional property (a?: T) vs a: T | undefined vs a: T | null

| a?: T | a: T | undefined | a: T | null
Can the key be missing? | Yes | No, you must write a: undefined | No
Reading it gives | T | undefined | T | undefined | T | null
Survives JSON | Missing key stays missing | Key dropped by JSON.stringify | Yes, sent as null
Means | "May not be provided" | "Must be passed, may be empty" | "Explicitly no value" (common from Java APIs)
Interview tip: a Spring Boot backend usually sends null for empty fields, so model those as T | null, not a?: T. Handle both at once with a ?? fallback.
TypeScript private vs JavaScript #private vs readonly

| private x | #x | readonly x
Checked by | Compiler only | JavaScript runtime | Compiler only
Accessible at runtime | Yes: obj['x'] or after casting to any | No, truly hidden | Yes, and writable via casts
Shown in console / JSON.stringify | Yes | No | Yes
Restricts | Who can read and write | Who can read and write | Writes after construction
Combine with | private readonly (Angular constructor injection) | readonly #x | Either
Rule of thumb: private is enough for normal encapsulation inside a TS codebase; use #x when the privacy must hold at runtime, for example in a library.
Type annotation vs as (assertion) vs non-null ! operator

| const u: User = … | … as User | value!
What it does | Checks the value fits the type | Tells the compiler "trust me" | Removes null | undefined from the type
Missing properties | Compile error | Allowed if the types overlap | n/a
Runtime check | None (types are erased) | None | None: it can still be null at runtime
Safe? | Yes | Only when you really know more than the compiler | Only right after a check the compiler cannot see
Rule of thumb: prefer annotations and type guards; treat every as and ! in a code review as a claim that needs a reason.
